articles.title: Senado deve votar nesta quarta PEC que acaba com a escala 6x1  | G1
articles.standfirst: Governistas e parlamentares da oposição dizem que há votos suficientes para aprovar a mudança na escala de trabalho no Brasil. Tema virou central nas campanhas dos dois candidatos à Presidência.
articles.summary: Governistas e parlamentares da oposição dizem que há votos suficientes para aprovar a mudança na escala de trabalho no Brasil. Tema virou central nas campanhas dos dois candidatos à Presidência.
articles.body:
Plenário do Senado Federal discute a PEC do fim da escala 6x1 — Foto: Jonas Pereira/Agência Senado

Após a quinta e última sessão de discussão, prevista para esta quarta-feira (14), o Senado deve votar, em primeiro e segundo turnos, a proposta que acaba com a escala 6x1 e prevê dois dias de folga remunerados por semana.

Isso porque o regimento prevê um intervalo de cinco dias úteis e a realização de outras três sessões de discussão. Os parlamentares, no entanto, podem apresentar um requerimento para dispensar esse intervalo ou reduzir o prazo.

Governistas e parlamentares da oposição dizem que há votos suficientes para aprovar a mudança na escala de trabalho no Brasil.

A ideia que circula no Senado é promulgar a PEC até quinta-feira (22), dias antes do segundo turno das eleições.

A primeira sessão de discussão da PEC ocorreu no dia 6 de outubro, dois dias depois do primeiro turno das eleições.

A maioria dos senadores do PL não participou da reunião do Senado sobre o tema. Senadores aliados de Flávio Bolsonaro tentaram esvaziar a discussão.

Marinho é autor de um texto que prevê a possibilidade de redução da jornada, com redução proporcional do salário.

A proposta foi aprovada pela Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) do Senado, em 2 de setembro.

A PEC do fim da jornada 6x1 altera a Constituição para diminuir as horas de trabalho semanais de 44 para 40 horas. Também estabelece que é necessário garantir dois dias de folga remunerada, um deles preferencialmente aos domingos.

Se aprovada, a PEC deve seguir a seguinte cronologia:

em dois meses, redução da jornada semanal para 42 horas, com dois dias de repouso semanal remunerado;

em um ano após esses dois meses, redução da jornada semanal para 40 horas.

A mudança não será aplicada para trabalhadores com ensino superior que ganhem por mês mais de 2,5 vezes o teto do INSS, ou seja, quem ganhe mais de R$ 21.188 por mês.

articles.summary: Pesquisa Quaest 2º turno traz intenções de voto entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro, além de índices de rejeição e avaliação do governo nesta quarta-feira.

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT) disputam o 2º turno — Foto: Diego Herculano/Reuters e Adriano Machado/Reuters

A Quaest divulga no final da tarde desta quarta-feira (14) sua primeira pesquisa de intenção de voto para o segundo turno da eleição presidencial de 2026. O levantamento foi encomendado pela Globo e pelo jornal O Globo.

📋 Segundo os dados registrados no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), foram entrevistadas 2.154 pessoas com 16 anos ou mais, entre os dias 10 e 13 de outubro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, com nível de confiança de 95%. A pesquisa está registrada no TSE sob o número BR-08729/2026.

Além das intenções de voto em Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e em Lula (PT), a Quaest também pesquisou sobre o voto no primeiro turno, níveis de rejeição aos candidatos, conhecimento sobre propostas dos presidenciáveis e avaliação do governo Lula.

Além da Quaest desta quarta-feira (14), o Datafolha também apresentará um novo levantamento sobre a disputa presidencial nesta semana. A pesquisa, encomendada pelo jornal Folha de S.Paulo, será divulgada na quinta-feira (15).

Na pesquisa anterior, divulgada na semana passada , Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) apareceu com 49% das intenções de voto, contra 45% de Lula (PT).

📋O novo levantamento do Datafolha prevê entrevistas com 2.520 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais, entre os dias 13 e 15 de outubro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. O registro no TSE é BR-00466/2026.

articles.title: Qual a diferença entre o primeiro e o segundo turno? | G1
articles.standfirst: O segundo turno ocorrerá no domingo (25) e eleitores do Brasil inteiro deverão escolher seu candidato a presidente. Em cinco estados e no DF, haverá também votação para governador.
articles.summary: O segundo turno ocorrerá no domingo (25) e eleitores do Brasil inteiro deverão escolher seu candidato a presidente. Em cinco estados e no DF, haverá também votação para governador.
articles.body:
Urna eletrônica — Foto: Giuliano Gomes/PR Press

No dia 25 de outubro, os mais de 158 milhões de eleitores habilitados no Brasil voltarão às urnas eletrônicas para o segundo turno das eleições.

Enquanto o primeiro turno abrange a votação para cargos do legislativo (deputados estaduais, federais e senadores) e executivo (presidente e governadores), o segundo turno é destinado exclusivamente à escolha dos chefes do poder executivo.

De acordo com a Constituição Federal , há segundo turno para a disputa da prefeitura quando os candidatos não conseguem alcançar a maioria absoluta dos votos válidos no primeiro turno – ou seja, 50% mais um.

Nesse caso, disputam o segundo turno os dois concorrentes mais votados na primeira etapa.

Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro disputam a cadeira de presidente. Além disso, apenas cinco estados e o Distrito Federal terão disputa de goverrnador em 2º turno. Quem mora nestes locais, portanto, devem votar em presidente e governador no dia 25:

Espírito Santo: Lorenzo Pazolini (Republicanos) e Ricardo Ferraço (MDB) vão disputar o 2º turno

Amazonas: Omar Aziz (PSD) e Professora Maria Do Carmo (PL) vão disputar o 2º turno

Rio Grande do Norte: Allyson (União) e Cadu De Lula (PT) vão disputar o 2º turno

Acre: Mailza Assis (Progressistas) e Alan Rick (Republicanos) vão disputar o 2º turno

Tocantins: Professora Dorinha (União) e Vicentinho Júnior (PSDB) vão disputar o 2º turno

Distrito Federal: Celina Leão (Progressistas) e Leandro Grass (PT) vão disputar o 2º turno

Para votar no segundo turno, o eleitor cumpre as mesmas regras que as observadas na primeira etapa da votação: é preciso ter em mãos documento original com foto, além de deixar o aparelho celular com o mesário antes de se dirigir à cabine de votação na sua zona e seção eleitoral.

Os eleitores podem conferir o local de votação no documento do título de eleitor, no aplicativo e-Título ou pelo 'Autoatendimento Eleitoral', no site do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), clicando na Onde votar e preenchendo os dados solicitados.

No site do TSE, é possível encontrar o local de votação. — Foto: Reprodução

IMPORTANTE: Os eleitores aptos que não votaram na primeira etapa de votação das Eleições Municipais de 2024, ocorrido em 6 de outubro, podem e devem participar do segundo turno .

A Justiça Eleitoral considera cada turno de votação uma eleição independente para efeito de comparecimento da eleitora ou do eleitor à urna eletrônica.

Ou seja: a ausência de comparecimento ao primeiro turno não impede os eleitores de exercerem o direito de voto na segunda etapa de votação.

articles.title: Aliados de Motta fazem contas para mantê-lo na presidência da Câmara e Centrão fala em ‘autopreservação’ | G1
articles.standfirst: Apesar de perfil mais à direita dos deputados eleitos, presidente da Câmara articula com aliados de partidos como PSD, PP e MDB, além de contar com apoio da esquerda.
articles.summary: Apesar de perfil mais à direita dos deputados eleitos, presidente da Câmara articula com aliados de partidos como PSD, PP e MDB, além de contar com apoio da esquerda.
articles.body:
O presidente da Câmara, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), durante reunião de líderes na Câmara — Foto: Kayo Magalhães/Câmara dos Deputados

Aliados do presidente da Câmara, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), avaliam que a disputa pela sucessão no comando da Casa está longe de estar definida . A eleição acontecerá em fevereiro do próximo ano, mas já é discutida nos bastidores em Brasília.

Apesar do crescimento da bancada da direita, aliados de Motta apostam que o Centrão fará um movimento de autoproteção para se preservar no poder e evitar que o bolsonarismo amplie sua influência sobre o Legislativo.

Nomes do Centrão lembram que, nos últimos anos, o Congresso ganhou força justamente por não ter um alinhamento automático com o Poder Executivo . Foi isso que permitiu, por exemplo, o avanço das emendas parlamentares.

Outro argumento é que a direita está avançando sobre as cadeiras de partidos do Centrão no Congresso. Por isso, não haveria interesse desses partidos de fortalecer, ainda mais, o PL.

“O PL cresceu, mas dificilmente terá, ao mesmo tempo, a presidência da República, da Câmara e do Senado, isso enfraqueceria todos os outros partidos”, diz um interlocutor do presidente da Câmara.

Algumas lideranças avaliam que o PL fez um cálculo errado ao já antecipar o interesse em comandar a Câmara e o Senado. O próprio senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) disse, publicamente, que o Congresso está "muito mais à direita do que ele é hoje".

"Com maioria no Senado para fazer o presidente do Senado, com maioria na Câmara para fazer o presidente da Câmara", disse Flávio na última semana, em um evento em Goiânia (GO).

As sinalizações do PL fizeram com que Motta ligasse o alerta antecipadamente e já começasse a articular a manutenção da sua cadeira. Segundo aliados, ele tem às mãos para negociar, por exemplo, a próxima vaga aberta no Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU), relatorias de propostas, distribuição de cargos na Mesa e nas comissões e a negociação sobre as emendas.

Nesta terça-feira (13), Motta já recebeu o apoio público do líder do PSD, Antonio Brito (BA), cuja bancada tem mais de 40 deputados. Sem cravar qual seria a contrapartida ao apoio, o presidente da Casa disse que "quem chega primeiro bebe água mais limpa" – em uma sinalização de que o PSD será bem contemplado nos acordos.

O líder do PSD na Câmara, deputado Antônio Brito (PSD-BA), em reunião de líder nesta terça-feira (13) — Foto: Kayo Magalhães/Câmara dos Deputados

O presidente da Câmara também tem se articulado em conversas com seus aliados de primeira hora. Entre eles, os líderes do PP, Dr. Luizinho (RJ), e do MDB, Isnaldo Bulhões (AL).

Além disso, a expectativa é que ele conte com o apoio de partidos como o Podemos e os partidos de esquerda (PT, PSB, PSOL, PCdoB, PDT, PV, Rede) que, juntos, terão 124 deputados federais.

Nos bastidores, aliados de Motta admitem que há uma resistência do PL ao nome dele. O partido conquistou 121 cadeiras, a a maior bancada desde a Constituição de 1988. Eles contam, porém, com o raciocínio de que, sozinho, o PL não consegue eleger um presidente da Câmara.

🔎 Para levar a vitória, é necessário ter a maioria absoluta entre os votantes. Se votam 500 deputados, por exemplo, se torna presidente da Câmara o candidato que receber 251 votos.

Esses interlocutores lembram que, quando Lula venceu a eleição de 2022, os partidos de esquerda reuniam cerca de 130 deputados e não tinham votos para garantir, por conta própria, o comando da Casa.

Nesse cenário, Motta teria mais a ganhar preservando a interlocução com diferentes campos políticos do que se alinhando integralmente ao eventual governo. A aposta é que, na próxima legislatura, a capacidade de reunir votos entre os próprios deputados será determinante para definir quem comandará a Câmara.

Ao anunciar apoio à eleição de Flávio , o deputado Marcos Pereira (Republicanos-SP), presidente da sigla, disse que, apesar do posicionamento do PL, o próprio Flávio não tem resistências a Hugo Motta.

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e integrantes do partido Republicanos durante anúncio de apoio no segundo turno — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Globo

Outro argumento colocado por aliados de Motta é que a prioridade da direita, neste momento, tem sido o comando do Senado. O senador e coordenador de campanha de Flávio, Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), não esconde que seu sonho político é chegar ao posto.

🕰️ No Congresso, existe a máxima de que o mesmo partido não costuma comandar as duas Casas. Ao longo dos anos, houve exceções: e m 2015, Renan Calheiros e Eduardo Cunha, ambos do PMDB (hoje MDB) ; e em 2019, Rodrigo Maia e Davi Alcolumbre, ambos do antigo DEM .

Apesar disso, a alternância de partidos na Casa tende a dar maior equilíbrio de poder entre os partidos e, por isso, é tida como praxe no Legislativo.

No Senado, o PL já soma 28 senadores . A conta deve subir com a saída de Cleitinho (Republicanos) para assumir o governo de Minas Gerais e a entrada de seu suplente, Alex Diniz (PL), além de outras filiações de senadores que o presidente do PL, Valdemar Costa Neto, vem prometendo.

O cenário torna a reeleição de Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP) na presidência do Senado mais desafiadora.

Além disso, alguns aliados de Motta avaliam que uma estratégia possível seria repetir a fórmula que garantiu a Arthur Lira (PP-AL) uma reeleição histórica na presidência da Casa em 2023.

Lira e Motta após resultado da eleição na Câmara em 2025 — Foto: Reprodução/TV Câmara

Eleito em 2021 com apoio do então presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL), Lira era apontado como um aliado de primeira ordem do bolsonarismo na Câmara. Com a vitória de Lula (PT) na eleição presidencial de 2022, houve dúvidas sobre sua capacidade de permanecer no comando da Casa.

Ainda na transição de governo, Lira entregou a Lula a PEC da Transição, que abriu espaço no Orçamento para as promessas do novo governo. Neste cenário, fez uma aliança do PT ao PL e conquistou 464 votos, a maior votação já registrada em uma eleição para a presidência da Câmara.

O presidente eleito, Lula, se encontrando com o então presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Arthur Lira, em 2022 — Foto: FáTIMA MEIRA/FUTURA PRESS/FUTURA PRESS/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

Interlocutores de Motta avaliam que não há motivo para reinventar a estratégia. A ideia é esperar o resultado do segundo turno da eleição presidencial e abrir uma rodada de conversas com as diferentes forças políticas para negociar apoio à sua permanência no cargo.

Se Flávio Bolsonaro vencer a disputa ao Planalto, Motta pode fazer acenos ao presidente eleito antes da posse, sob o argumento de que o cargo de presidente da Câmara exige capacidade de articulação com o governo.

O movimento teria de ser calculado para não perder os votos da esquerda, de quem Motta se aproximou. Na última quinta-feira (8), o presidente da Câmara se reuniu com o presidente Lula. Questionado sobre a conversa, Lula respondeu: “o Motta vai me ajudar a ganhar as eleições”.

Durante a eleição de primeiro turno, Motta pediu abertamente votos para o presidente Lula – movimento visto como uma tentativa de eleger seu pai, Nabor Wanderley (Republicanos), ao Senado pela Paraíba, estado que historicamente vota com o petista. Nabor, porém, não foi eleito.

Parte dos deputados avalia que o posicionamento de Motta de apoio a Lula pode dificultar suas chances de reeleição, em caso de vitória de Flávio.

Seus aliados fazem uma leitura diferente: manter as pontes com o governo Lula pode ser decisivo para conquistar os votos da esquerda, independentemente do resultado da eleição presidencial. Afinal, agora, os votos que contam são os de seus colegas parlamentares.

articles.title: CCJ do Senado pode concluir nesta quarta votação da PEC da Segurança | G1
articles.standfirst: Senadores não analisaram três trechos do texto da proposta em separado, chamados destaques. Caso votação seja finalizada, proposta segue para análise do Plenário do Senado.
articles.summary: Senadores não analisaram três trechos do texto da proposta em separado, chamados destaques. Caso votação seja finalizada, proposta segue para análise do Plenário do Senado.
articles.body:
A Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) do Senado pode concluir nesta quarta-feira (14) a análise da Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) da Segurança Pública. Os senadores ainda precisam votar três destaques ao texto principal, etapa que ficou pendente após a aprovação da proposta pelo colegiado no mês passado.

A PEC foi aprovada pela comissão em 2 de setembro , mas a votação não foi concluída porque parlamentares deixaram para uma sessão posterior a análise de trechos apresentados separadamente.

Após a deliberação desses destaques, a proposta segue para análise do plenário do Senado.

Entre os pontos pendentes está uma emenda do senador Alessandro Vieira (MDB-SE) que altera regras para as polícias municipais.

A proposta retira a exigência de acreditação periódica por conselhos estaduais de segurança pública, prevista no texto aprovado pela Câmara, e prevê que a atuação dessas corporações siga parâmetros nacionais definidos em lei federal.

Na prática, a proposta busca evitar que a atuação de um órgão municipal fique condicionada à avaliação periódica de uma instância estadual.

Também aguardam votação duas emendas do senador Carlos Portinho (PL-RJ).

Uma delas inclui expressamente os agentes de trânsito entre os órgãos de segurança pública previstos na Constituição. A outra autoriza o uso de recursos do Fundo Nacional de Segurança Pública em ações específicas das Forças Armadas, como operações de combate a crimes transfronteiriços e ambientais e missões de Garantia da Lei e da Ordem (GLO).

Considerada uma das prioridades do governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), a PEC estabelece na Constituição o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública (Susp), com o objetivo de ampliar a integração entre União, estados e Distrito Federal no combate ao crime organizado.

O presidente já disse que espera a aprovação da PEC para a criação do Ministério de Segurança Pública e promete uma atuação mais direta do governo federal contra o crime organizado.

Comissão de Constituição, Justiça e Cidadania (CCJ) realiza reunião com 12 itens — Foto: Edilson Rodrigues/Agência Senado

A proposta estabelece na Constituição o Sistema Úico de Segurança Pública (SUSP), cujo objetivo é integrar o combate ao crime organizado entre os entes.

De acordo com o texto, União, Estados e Distrito Federal poderão criar leis na área de segurança pública, incluindo forças-tarefa intergovernamentais, organização das polícias e guardas municipais e do sistema socioeducativo.

Segundo o relator, esse é um ponto central da PEC. "É preciso colocar os entes federados e as forças de segurança pública para colaborarem entre si, não para competirem", diz Carvalho em seu parecer.

Outro ponto central da PEC da Segurança Pública é sobre o combate a crimes violentos e facções criminosas.

Entre as medidas estão a obrigatoriedade de prisão em estabelecimento penal de segurança máxima ou de natureza especial.

Também fica proibida ou restringida a progressão de regime, a concessão de liberdade provisória, com ou sem fiança, e de saída temporária.

A PEC também permite a expropriação de todo e qualquer bem, direito ou valor econômico envolvido com as atividades criminosas. As regras valem para organizações criminosas, paramilitares e de milícia privada.

criação de polícias municipais para o policiamento ostensivo e comunitário;

ampliação da atuação da Polícia Rodoviária Federal (PRF) para o policiamento de hidrovias e ferrovias, além de apoiar outras forças de segurança, quando requisitada pelo governador;

manter Polícia Federal e PRF sob competência privativa da União, assim como as normas para atividades de inteligência.

articles.title: Fim da escala 6x1: Senado decide hoje futuro da PEC | G1
articles.standfirst: A proposta precisa de pelo menos 49 votos favoráveis para avançar no Senado. Entenda o que acontece em caso de rejeição, quais etapas ainda faltam e quando as mudanças poderiam entrar em vigor.
articles.summary: A proposta precisa de pelo menos 49 votos favoráveis para avançar no Senado. Entenda o que acontece em caso de rejeição e quais etapas ainda faltam.
articles.body:
Sessão de Debates - Fim da escala 6x1 no Brasil. — Foto: Edilson Rodrigues/Agência Senado

A Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) que prevê o fim da escala 6x1 enfrenta nesta quarta-feira (14) uma das votações mais importantes de sua tramitação no Congresso Nacional.

Após ser aprovada em dois turnos pela Câmara dos Deputados e receber parecer favorável da Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) do Senado, a proposta será submetida à votação no plenário da Casa .

➡️ O resultado poderá colocar o texto a poucos passos de uma mudança na Constituição Federal ou interromper completamente seu avanço no Legislativo. Para continuar tramitando, a PEC precisará receber pelo menos 49 votos favoráveis entre os 81 senadores.

A votação tem mobilizado parlamentares, trabalhadores e representantes do setor produtivo porque poderá definir os rumos de uma proposta que altera a jornada máxima de trabalho prevista na Constituição Federal, reduzindo o limite semanal de 44 para 40 horas e garantindo dois dias de descanso remunerado por semana sem redução salarial.

Mas, afinal, uma eventual rejeição significa o fim definitivo da proposta? Ela poderia voltar ao Congresso no futuro? E, se for aprovada, quanto ainda falta para que as novas regras entrem em vigor?

A seguir, veja o que está em jogo na votação desta quarta-feira.

Os senadores devem realizar a quinta e última sessão de discussão da proposta prevista no regimento interno e, antes da análise da PEC, votar um requerimento de calendário especial que pode acelerar sua tramitação.

O pedido, apresentado pela líder do governo no Senado, Teresa Leitão (PT-PE), recebeu as 54 assinaturas necessárias para ser analisado pelo plenário. Se for aprovado, permitirá que a proposta seja votada em primeiro e segundo turnos no mesmo dia, reduzindo etapas regimentais normalmente exigidas entre as duas votações.

Por se tratar de uma PEC, o texto precisa do apoio de três quintos dos integrantes da Casa para ser aprovado. No Senado, isso corresponde a pelo menos 49 votos favoráveis.

A votação desta quarta poderá ser decisiva para o futuro da proposta . Caso o calendário especial seja aprovado e a PEC alcance os votos necessários nos dois turnos, o Senado poderá concluir sua análise ainda nesta semana.

A discussão ocorre após semanas de negociações envolvendo governo, oposição e representantes de diferentes setores econômicos.

A votação desta quarta-feira vai definir se a PEC continuará avançando ou se terá a tramitação encerrada ainda em 2026.

Segundo o professor de Direito Constitucional da USP Rubens Beçak, uma PEC precisa ser aprovada em dois turnos, por maioria qualificada, na Câmara e no Senado. Se for rejeitada em qualquer uma dessas etapas, a proposta é arquivada.

"Havendo uma rejeição em qualquer dos turnos agora no Senado, a proposta é arquivada nesta legislatura."

📎 Isso não significa, porém, que o fim da escala 6x1 deixaria de ser discutido. A rejeição encerraria a tramitação da PEC atual, mas uma nova proposta poderia ser apresentada em legislaturas posteriores . Também seria possível tentar mudanças na jornada de trabalho por outros instrumentos legislativos, afirma Beçak.

"Às vezes avança-se por um caminho que não dá certo. Daí se procura regulamentar por outro."

O professor ressalta que, no momento, não há uma proposta concreta em tramitação por esse caminho.

Se a proposta obtiver os votos necessários, ela continuará avançando normalmente no Senado.

⚠️ A aprovação em primeiro turno não altera imediatamente a Constituição nem muda as regras da jornada de trabalho.

Na prática, ela apenas permite que o texto avance para a reta final do processo legislativo.

Depois dessa etapa, ainda será necessária a aprovação em segundo turno, novamente com pelo menos 49 votos favoráveis.

O requerimento de calendário especial apresentado por líderes partidários pode reduzir o intervalo normalmente exigido entre as duas votações.

Se esse pedido for aprovado pelo plenário, os senadores poderão realizar o segundo turno ainda nesta quarta-feira, concluindo a análise da proposta no Senado.

Sim. Apesar de o relator da matéria, senador Omar Aziz (PSD-AM), ter rejeitado as 36 emendas apresentadas até o momento, novas sugestões de alteração ainda podem ser apresentadas durante a tramitação em plenário.

Caso alguma mudança seja aprovada, a PEC deixará de ter a mesma redação que passou pela Câmara.

Nessa hipótese, o texto precisará retornar aos deputados federais para uma nova análise antes da promulgação, o que poderá prolongar o processo legislativo.

A votação final pode ocorrer ainda em outubro?

A depender da aprovação do calendário especial, a votação final poderá ocorrer já nesta quarta-feira .

Pelas regras normais do Senado, a PEC precisa aguardar um intervalo entre os dois turnos de votação, além de novas sessões de discussão em plenário.

➡️ Parlamentares favoráveis à proposta, porém , conseguiram as assinaturas necessárias para apresentar um requerimento que permite abreviar esse rito . O presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), informou que o pedido deverá ser analisado antes da votação da PEC.

Se o calendário especial for aprovado e a proposta alcançar os 49 votos necessários nos dois turnos, o Senado encerrará a tramitação da matéria ainda nesta semana.

Nesse cenário, caso o texto seja aprovado sem alterações em relação à versão enviada pela Câmara dos Deputados, a p roposta seguirá diretamente para promulgação, sem necessidade de nova análise dos deputados .

A expectativa de parlamentares favoráveis à medida é que a emenda constitucional seja promulgada até o dia 22 de outubro.

Diferentemente dos projetos de lei, as propostas de emenda à Constituição não dependem de sanção ou veto do presidente da República.

"Terminando o fluxo, ela é promulgada. Não é o caso de lei que depende de sanção presidencial", pontua Beçak.

A PEC 221/2019 altera o artigo 7º da Constituição Federal para reduzir a jornada máxima semanal de trabalho no Brasil.

Hoje, o limite constitucional é de 44 horas semanais. O texto aprovado pela Câmara reduz esse teto para 40 horas, sem permitir redução salarial.

A proposta também garante dois dias de descanso remunerado por semana e determina preferência para que um deles seja concedido aos domingos.

Na prática, a mudança elimina a possibilidade de adoção da escala 6x1 como modelo regular de jornada.

O texto mantém o limite máximo de oito horas de trabalho por dia e preserva os pisos salariais das categorias.

As mudanças passariam a valer imediatamente?

Não. A PEC prevê uma implementação gradual para permitir a adaptação de empresas e trabalhadores.

Iniciada 60 dias após a promulgação da emenda:

redução da jornada máxima de 44 para 42 horas semanais;

garantia de dois dias de descanso remunerado por semana.

redução definitiva da jornada máxima para 40 horas semanais.

Na prática, a implementação completa ocorreria cerca de 14 meses após a promulgação da emenda constitucional.

A medida alcançaria a maior parte dos trabalhadores contratados pelo regime da Consolidação das Leis do Trabalho (CLT).

O texto, porém, prevê exceções e regras específicas.

Atividades contínuas e consideradas essenciais, como saúde, segurança, transporte e limpeza urbana, poderão manter escalas diferenciadas por meio de acordos e convenções coletivas.

A proposta também estabelece tratamento diferenciado para trabalhadores com diploma de ensino superior que recebam remuneração superior a 2,5 vezes o teto do INSS, atualmente em torno de R$ 21 mil mensais.

Além disso, determina que uma futura lei complementar estabeleça regras específicas para microempreendedores individuais (MEIs), microempresas e empresas de pequeno porte.

articles.title: In heated Georgia Senate debate, Jon Ossoff says he won’t run for president in 2028
articles.summary: The Democratic incumbent pledged to serve a full term as he and challenger Rep. Mike Collins hit on similar themes as in their first debate last week.
articles.body:
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said Tuesday night during a debate that he will not run for president in 2028.

Ossoff made the statement in response to a question as he faced off with his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff is seeking a second six-year term in Georgia and said he would serve the full term.

"I have zero interest in running for president," Ossoff said when he was asked directly by one of the moderators. "I'm not running for president. I'm running for re-election to the Senate."

Ossoff has been regularly discussed as a potential Democratic contender in 2028. If he were to win the presidency, he would have to give up his Senate seat, which he stressed Tuesday night that he would not do.

After the brief remark, Ossoff quickly transitioned to pressing Collins about why he has supported President Donald Trump's tariffs, a main focus of both his campaign and a debate the two held last week . Tuesday was the second debate in the nationally watched Georgia Senate race, this one organized by the Atlanta Press Club.

Collins quipped that Ossoff was actually trying to run for president and will be "your DSA candidate," a reference to the Democratic Socialists of America.

The exchange came at the beginning of the hourlong debate, which covered ground including data centers; the economy under Trump, whose approval rating is at record lows; the war in Iran; and the issue of Collins' son-in-law's promoting white nationalist posts on social media.

Ossoff asked Collins directly whether he considered himself a "white nationalist."

"I condemn any sort of hate speech," Collins said. "Antisemitism, hate of any kind. It's abhorrent."

The exchange continued when Collins again asked Ossoff to denounce Reid Hoffman, a major donor to Democratic causes — including Ossoff-aligned political committees — whose name appeared in the Epstein files . Collins brought up Hoffman several times last week and did so again during the second debate.

Ossoff did not directly respond, and he again pointed to the fact that those close to Collins amplified white nationalists' posts.

"How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for Senate?" Ossoff said. "The paper reported it's still going on today."

Given a chance to respond, Collins did not address it directly. But he said rhetoric like Ossoff's had motivated a New York man who is accused of making death threats against him.

"I'm a little tired of this, Jon," Collins said. "This crazy person is in jail right now because of your rhetoric."

Neither candidate directly answered the other's charges.

Collins also, once again, did not answer questions about whether or not Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. He was asked about audio of a call Trump made after the 2020 election asking Georgia Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to " find 11,780 votes " to help overturn the 2020 election.

"You know, Joe Biden went into office, and boy, Georgians paid for it," Collins said.

articles.body:
President Trump announced Tuesday that Taiwan has agreed to purchase 30 percent of gas from the Alaska pipeline over the next 20 years.

Speaking at a campaign rally in Wasilla, Alaska, Trump said Taiwan will invest $4.4 billion into the project on top of $50 billion already committed by South Korea.

The president was quick to credit incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), who is facing a competitive election bid, with the announcement.

“I have to say that Dan Sullivan helped me get this done. Thank you, Dan,” Trump said at the event.

Earlier this month, Trump announced South Korea would invest up to $200 billion into U.S. energy infrastructure, including toward a natural gas pipeline in Alaska. The investment also sought to fund a natural gas plant in Texas and eight new nuclear power plants across the U.S.

“The United States is already the largest natural gas producer and exporter in the world, and this pipeline will help us expand those exports even further,” Trump said, speaking alongside Sullivan in the Oval Office earlier this month.

Rising energy prices resulting from the U.S.’s war in Iran has hit states like Alaska hard ahead of the midterms.

Sullivan is facing a competitive reelection bid against former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska). The incumbent senator is also running against another Republican in the race, who is also named Dan Sullivan.

Trump’s decision to journey out to the state during the midterm season underscores how critical the red leaning state will be on Election Day.

Sabato’s Crystal Ball, an election handicapper based at the University of Virginia, moved the race from “toss-up” to “leans Democratic” earlier this week.

Decision Desk HQ, another election handicapper, also has Peltola slightly favored to win, while the Cook Political Report has the race in the “toss-up” category.

articles.title: Collins, Jackson duke it out in third Maine Senate debate: 3 takeaways
articles.summary: Republican Sen. Susan Collins (R) and Democrat Troy Jackson clashed Tuesday in their third Maine Senate debate with just three weeks until Election Day. Collins and Jackson sparred on several topics, including the incumbent’s votes for and against the Iran war as well as their differing views on how to address cost of living issues…
articles.body:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins (R) and Democrat Troy Jackson clashed Tuesday in their third Maine Senate debate with just three weeks until Election Day.

Collins and Jackson sparred on several topics, including the incumbent’s votes for and against the Iran war as well as their differing views on how to address cost of living issues in the Pine Tree State, over the course of the hour-long debate hosted by Maine station WABI.

At times they found common ground, however,on their opposition to President Trump’s trade war with Canada as well as data centers. But Jackson still regularly sought to tie Collins to Trump and his agenda, prompting pushback from the senator.

The two candidates will face off once again on Thursday in a debate moderated by News Center Maine .

Here are three takeaways from their latest face-off:

Jackson zeroes in on Trump as Collins seeks distance

Jackson repeatedly sought to link Collins to Trump, as his sagging approval ratings threaten to bog down Republicans up and down the ballot in November.

On the Iran war, Jackson accused the senator of voting to support Trump’s military authorization “because she does whatever Donald Trump wants.”

“And when Susan Collins had the chance to stop him, because she’s chair of [the Senate Appropriations Committee], she would not do that,” Jackson said. “And that’s where we are right now.”

Collins pushed back, noting she broke with her conference and voted nine times to end the conflict under the War Powers Act. The Maine Republican did vote on five occasions against failed resolutions to rein in Trump’s war powers earlier this year.

Jackson linked the Iran war to rising energy prices, continuing to knock Collins for not pushing back enough against the president. Collins cast the blame on the Maine state legislature in Augusta for high energy costs for Mainers. Jackson was the state Senate’s president until 2024.

The Democrat also sought to tie Collins to Trump while debating tariffs on Canada. He said that lawmakers in Washington should have intervened and used their authority to stop the tariff.

“The bottom line is that Troy and I both would have voted against the Canadian tariffs,” Collins replied. “There would have been no difference in our votes on those issues. But here’s the key difference. I’ve been able to negotiate and get certain items removed from the tariff list.”

Jackson says he’ll release FEC report before next debate

Collins raised concerns over Jackson’s Federal Election Commission (FEC) report “outlining his contributors and his expenditures,” prompting the Democrat to say he will release the filings.

“He’s yet to tell us. He promised to be completely transparent, yet he has not filed a single report,” Collins said.

On the campaign trail, Collins has scrutinized Jackson over his financial disclosures, particularly given his populist campaign and his public rejection of corporate PAC money. Jackson told Collins on the debate stage that he would release the filing publicly Wednesday morning.

“How about that? Was that enough?” he added. “Because we see yours and I know that there’s no billionaires funding me.”

The deadline for Q3 federal campaign expenditure filings is late Thursday. Collins has not yet released her report for the same time period.

Earlier, Jackson jabbed the senator over September ProPublica reporting that the FBI investigated a pay-for-play scheme that Collins and her super PAC allegedly engaged in with a defense contractor. The senator has denied the report , ripping it as a “partisan hit job.”

Jackson said during Tuesday’s debate that he was shocked to hear Collins talk about routing out fraud at the state level because “there’s only one person up here that’s been accused of that by the FBI.”

The remark was brushed off by Collins, who later accused him of lying and attacking her integrity.

Towards the end of the debate, Collins accused her opponent of having “repeatedly insulted my integrity all evening long.”

“He claims that I do what the so-called billionaires want to do … And I just cannot continue to ignore these attacks on my integrity,” she said.

Candidates find common ground on Canada tariffs, data centers

The Maine Senate candidates found some common ground at their third meeting on the debate stage

Both of them sharply disagreed with the White House’s tariffs on Canada after failed talks between both countries, with Collins saying, “Troy and I both would have voted against the Canadian tariffs.”

“Well, it wasn’t the Canadians that started this problem,” Collins said. “It was the Trump administration. Now the Canadians do have trade barriers when it comes to dairy products and I have advised the Canadian ambassador that they should get rid of that.”

Jackson argued Collins could have done more to prevent the tariffs, adding that the levies are “one man’s foolishness” and “that we’re dealing with in this state, and “it’s costing so many more people money than it should have.”

“Blanket tariffs are never going to be something I’ll ever support,” he said.

The two also largely agreed on data centers. Collins pointed to her support for the Ratepayer Protection Act, which sought to mitigate high energy costs associated with the development of these facilities. She noted that she thinks data center contruction should “be a local decision”

Jackson agreed that there needs to be guardrails in place on development, though he knocked Collins on leaving it at the local level.

I am very much in favor of making sure that either the federal government or the state of Maine puts guardrails on these things because I don’t want the billionaires, again, writing the rules and making our communities worse off than they are right now,” he added.

Collins retorted, adding that it “sounds like Troy and I, oddly enough, are not that far apart on this issue.”

articles.title: Trump pardons diesel mechanics for Clean Air Act violations at Alaska rally
articles.summary: President Trump issued pardons at a campaign rally in Alaska on Tuesday for two diesel mechanics who were previously charged with and plead guilty to violating the Clean Air Act. The president signed the pardons for Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming on stage at the campaign event in Wasilla after he invited then up on…
articles.body:
President Trump issued pardons at a campaign rally in Alaska on Tuesday for two diesel mechanics who were previously charged with and plead guilty to violating the Clean Air Act.

The president signed the pardons for Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming on stage at the campaign event in Wasilla after he invited then up on stage.

“They wanted to put them in jail for 10 years because they fixed an engine, how sick,” Trump said.

“The concept is that if you allow people to fix the engines, they’re going to take all of the environmental crap that makes it bad, makes it expensive, that they’re going to do undo that. And when you undo that, you therefore send fumes into the air, so we’re going to put them in jail for ten years,” he continued.

Czubak and Fleming each plead guilty in 2022 to federal charges that they violated the Clean Air Act by illegally tampering with equipment and removed equipment meant to control air pollution.

According to the Anchorage Daily News, federal prosecutors said the two men and along with Michael Wayne Hanzuk tampered with and removed emission controls from at least 37 vehicles between July 2019 and September 2020.

“This means the world to me,” Fleming said on stage. “We’re not criminals. We’re not trying to hurt anybody. We want to help Alaskans. We want to help people with diesel trucks, with vehicles across the world.”

Trump previously pardoned nine convicted of similar Clean Air Act violations in July for what a White House official described as overzealous enforcement by previous administrations.

articles.title: Ossoff, Collins clash in second Georgia Senate debate: 4 takeaways
articles.summary: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) and Rep. Mike Collins (R) traded barbs in a Tuesday night debate, tangling over the Jeffrey Epstein files, the 2020 election and more. Ossoff, the only Senate Democrat running for reelection in a state President Trump won in 2024, tied his Republican opponent to the administration’s controversial tariffs and war in…
articles.body:
Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) and Rep. Mike Collins (R) traded barbs in a Tuesday night debate, tangling over the Jeffrey Epstein files, the 2020 election and more.

Ossoff, the only Senate Democrat running for reelection in a state President Trump won in 2024, tied his Republican opponent to the administration’s controversial tariffs and war in Iran. Collins, backed by Trump, sought to paint Ossoff as more representative of “Georgetown” in Washington than Georgia, suggesting the Democrat is “using this as a platform” for future political moves.

With early voting underway, Ossoff is leading Collins by nearly 10 percentage points in Decision Desk HQ’s latest polling averages on the race, and Cook Political Report shifted the contest toward Democrats last month .

But Republicans aren’t giving up on a flip in the Peach State. Trump is headed to Georgia on Friday to campaign for Collins as part of a red-state swing to rev up Republican voters.

Tuesday’s face-off was the last scheduled debate in the Georgia Senate race, hosted by the Atlanta Press Club. Here are four takeaways:

Ossoff commits to full Senate term if reelected

Ossoff committed on Tuesday to serving a full six-year Senate term and reiterated that he has “zero interest” in a 2028 presidential campaign, despite chatter about the first-term senator’s political future.

“Yes, I will,” Ossoff said, when asked to pledge his commitment serving a full term if he wins the race in November.

“I have zero interest in running for president. I’m not running for president. I’m running for re-election to the Senate.”

Ossoff, who won his first term in a high-profile 2020 cycle runoff , has long denied speculation about a possible presidential run, though that hasn’t stopped observers from looking to the rising political star as a potential standard-bearer for the party.

Democrats have notably seen similarities in the political rhetoric and style of both Ossoff and former President Obama — who famously said in 2006 that he would not run for the presidency as he served out his Senate term in Illinois, but later backtracked and ran in the 2008 cycle.

Collins on the debate stage pushed back against Ossoff’s answer, saying “he is running for president. He’s going to be your DSA candidate,” in a reference to this cycle’s string of far-left Democratic Socialist of America (DSA) wins. Ossoff is not a DSA member.

Collins again refuses to say Trump lost 2020 election

Collins repeatedly sidestepped questions from moderators and his Senate rival about President Trump’s unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud in the 2020 presidential election.

“Do you still believe that Trump defeated Joe Biden in 2020?” said the Atlanta Journal-Constitution’s Greg Bluestein.

“Yeah, you know, Joe Biden went into office, and boy, Georgians paid for it. Look at what happened during the Biden years,” the congressman said.

Later, Ossoff pressed Collins for not answering earlier, re-asking whether Trump won the 2020 election.

“You know, the 2020 election. Everybody’s seen my, my views on that,” Collins said. “There was a lot of doubt in that election. Yes, Joe Biden was the president.”

Ossoff pressed that he didn’t hear an answer to the question, and raised it again later in the debate.

“You still haven’t answered tonight whether you believe Donald Trump actually won the 2020 election. Here’s your third chance. Did Donald Trump really win the 2020 election? You want to answer, Mike?”

“I have said numerous times that Joe Biden was the president in 2021,” Collins replied.

Trump has continued to challenge the results of the 2020 election , when he narrowly lost Georgia to former President Biden and put pressure on Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger (R) and other officials to overturn the results.

The candidates clashed over alleged ties and files related to Epstein, the convicted sex offender and disgraced financier who died in prison in 2019.

Collins said that ads for Ossoff were paid for by Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire and major Democratic donor with ties to Epstein. After Trump launched an investigation into a number of Democrats with such ties, Hoffman said last year that he was “never a client of Epstein’s and never had any engagement with him other than fundraising for MIT,” referring to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

“Jon, the call’s coming from the inside the house. The Epstein class that you’re talking about? I’m looking at him right now,” Collins said.

But Ossoff pushed back by pointing to Collins’s votes on releasing Epstein-related files.

“Mike, who on your team advised you to raise the Epstein files? You voted to cover up the evidence,” Ossoff pushed back later in the debate, noting that Trump is named multiple times in the Epstein files. “You should explain that vote to Jeffrey Epstein’s victims right now.”

Ossoff signals openness to packing Supreme Court

Ossoff signaled he’s open to packing the Supreme Court, but stressed that the priority should be on a code of ethics for justices.

“I don’t rule out any judicial reform, but I think we have to take the long view whenever we consider anything like that,” the senator said when asked about the topic should Democrats clinch the Senate.

“I think our focus should be a binding code of ethics for Supreme Court justices, because the American public is rightly offended when they see Supreme Court justices accepting lavish gifts from people who have business before the court, or from people who have a record of ideological or partisan advocacy.”

As he ran for the office in 2020, Ossoff said he was opposed to adding more seats to the nation’s highest court.

“I think judicial reform is a prerogative of Congress, and what I don’t support is adding a seat to the Supreme Court because we don’t like the policy positions of a justice that has been confirmed,” Ossoff said at the time.

The Democrat also called on Tuesday for a “much stronger” ethical code in Congress, where Collins’s office is under federal investigation from the House Ethics Committee for alleged misuse of tax dollars.

Collins, though, said he’s “fully complied” with the probe and called it a “nothing burger” and “just a hit job.”

articles.body:
NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo on Tuesday questioned former White House adviser Steve Bannon about if he will accept the outcome of the midterm elections if Democrats defeat Republicans.

“I want to ask you straight, here on the record,” Cuomo began before asking Bannon if the GOP lost key races, “will you accept the results of the election?” during a town hall event on NewsNation, the Hill’s sister network, on Tuesday night.

“We have to first off — let’s have the election first,” Bannon responded.

Bannon then added later that “they certified an illegitimate election in 2020,” bringing up an unfounded claim that President Trump won that year’s presidential election.

“I went to prison for that,” Bannon said. “I’m proud I went to prison for that.”

“You went to prison because you wouldn’t testify,” Cuomo replied. “That’s why you went to prison.”

Bannon retorted that his prison sentence was “about the 2020 election, Chris, thank you very much,” adding that he “wouldn’t bend the knee to [former House Speaker] Nancy Pelosi [(D-Calif.)].”

“You wouldn’t bend the knee to democracy,” Cuomo shot back.

Bannon was served a four-month prison sentence about two years ago for refusing to comply with a congressional subpoena related to the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol.

The former White House adviser’s comments come as Democrats appear poised to make gains in both the House and Senate in this year’s midterm elections. Decision Desk HQ has forecasted that following the elections, the Democrats will retake the Senate and House with 51 seats and 235 seats, respectively.

Trump and his party are facing rocky political territory as Election Day creeps closer, with the unpopular war in Iran raging on for months, the president’s approval rating sagging and notable concerns about the cost of living.

articles.body:
Iowa Senate GOP candidate Ashley Hinson said on Tuesday that she didn’t agree with a recent deal President Trump struck with Russia that would import 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global marketplace, taking issue with the U.S. making a deal with an adversary.

“We need to lower gas prices in this country. We need to lower diesel prices, but I don’t think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it,” Hinson said during the second televised Iowa Senate debate hosted by WHO 13, an affiliate of Nexstar, which also owns The Hill.

“I think we should be doing it by lowering the gas tax temporarily, making sure we’re actually looking at potentially a diesel rebate program for our producers, investing in America’s biofuels, which is the homegrown answer that we have right here in Iowa,” she added.

The president announced a deal last week that Russia had agreed to import 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global marketplace as Trump looks to quickly reverse high gas prices just weeks out from the election.

The deal prompted bipartisan blowback, including a letter signed by six GOP senators and released on Tuesday that criticized the president for striking the deal with Russia.

Hinson told The Associated Press earlier on Tuesday that “It makes me a little bit nervous anytime we’re talking about relieving a sanction on Russia.”

Turek quipped it was a rare issue where the two of them agreed, saying he also didn’t support a diesel deal with Russia.

“We actually agree on this. I want to do everything that I can because everywhere I’m going, all across Iowa, I’m hearing from Iowans talking about gas prices and diesel prices,” Turek said. “But I don’t think it should be at the expense of benefiting the economy of someone like a Vladimir Putin, who we clearly cannot trust.”

The issue has become an awkward issue for other Senate candidates, including South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham (R), who did not say during a debate with Democrat Annie Andrews over the weekend whether she agreed with the president’s deal.

“I think that everybody wants the war in Ukraine to end. We will all be safer when the war in Ukraine ends,” Graham said during the debate .

She said she was “proud” to help pass legislation that had enacted sanctions on Russian energy buyers.

“It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses to end the war through economic sanctions. So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it or whether he wants to use something else,” she said. “But I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.”

Last month, Hinson declared that Iowans “shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” a notable acknowledgment by a GOP candidate in a key battleground state that President Trump’s foreign policy is hitting Americans hard in the wallet.

articles.title: Judge extends order allowing CNN, Politico, MS NOW White House press access
articles.summary: A federal judge on Tuesday issued a longer block on President Trump’s ban of three major news organizations from the White House, finding that the revocation of the outlets’ hard badges likely violated their constitutional rights. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly wrote in a late-night ruling that the preliminary injunction was meant to preserve the…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Tuesday issued a longer block on President Trump’s ban of three major news organizations from the White House, finding that the revocation of the outlets’ hard badges likely violated their constitutional rights.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly wrote in a late-night ruling that the preliminary injunction was meant to preserve the “status quo” while CNN, Politico and MS NOW’s lawsuit continues.

The Trump-appointed judge found that the three outlets were likely to succeed in their claims that the administration engaged in viewpoint discrimination and retaliation when it excluded them from the White House. He reiterated an earlier ruling that the outlets were likely not given enough due process.

“For all the reasons explained elsewhere, it is likely that Plaintiffs were selected by President Trump for revocation of their access to the White House press area because he believes their coverage of him and his administration is generally inaccurate and biased,” Kelly wrote.

“Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination,” the judge added.

The outlets sued the Trump administration after they were barred from access the White House grounds last month, arguing that it was designed to punish them for what the president viewed as unfavorable coverage. Lawyers pointed to Trump’s suggestion that the decision was based on cumulative negative coverage rather than individual stories as evidence.

The Justice Department cited national security concerns as the justification for the media access restrictions, with the administration criticizing the use of anonymous sources and accuses the outlets of being “fake news.”

“The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound,” Ted Boutrous, an attorney representing the outlets said in a statement. “The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future.”

Kelly cautioned that his Tuesday order should not be interpreted to “suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded” or that the government cannot take any action when its “true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”

Still, the judge rejected the notion that national security was the driving rationale behind the president’s decision.

“There is no evidence in the record that President Trump made the decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ hard passes on national security grounds from the get-go, nor at any time has he directly stated that national security was the reason for his decision.”

This was the second time Kelly has ruled in the case, having previously handed down a temporary restraining order that required the administration to immediately restore CNN, Politico and MS NOW’s access.

The order comes as the feud between Trump and the media has only ramped up, with the Justice Department announcing over the weekend that it was opening an antitrust investigation into the five major television networks after they temporarily suspended press pool coverage during the ban.

articles.title: Federal judge issues longer-term decision blocking Trump’s White House media ban
articles.summary: U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued an injunction preventing CNN, Politico and MS NOW from being booted from the White House grounds until the case is decided.
articles.body: A federal judge issued an order late Tuesday blocking the Trump administration from banning CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House complex while the organizations’ lawsuit over access proceeds. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly of Washington, D.C., issued the preliminary injunction in the wake of a hearing Thursday at which the administration contended it imposed the ban in part because of national security concerns; media organizations said it was because of “viewpoint discrimination.” Kelly sided with the news outlets, noting that Trump used national security as a reason for the ban after their press passes had already been revoked and ruling that it also likely violated reporters’ freedom of speech and due process rights. “There is practically nothing national security-related in the record connected to the President’s decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ hard passes to which the Court can defer,” Kelly wrote in his 26-page opinion. His order will give the outlets access to the White House until the underlying lawsuit challenging the ban is resolved. But it doesn’t require the administration to allow reporters from the outlets access to the Oval Office or Air Force One — locations where the administration has blocked reporters from CNN and Politico in recent weeks. Trump vowed to appeal on Truth Social before the ruling was handed down. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment following the ruling. Kelly had issued a temporary restraining order lifting the ban while he weighed whether to issue an injunction. Trump announced the bans of CNN, MS NOW and Politico on social media on Sept. 18, saying they were a “result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he wrote on Truth Social. In court filings, the three news organizations said the ban affected 78 journalists who had “hard passes,” meaning they had been previously screened and credentialed to work at the White House. The outlets filed a lawsuit alleging Trump’s action violated their due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech. “This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the suit said. The White House and Trump then began arguing that the ban was intended to address national security concerns, with Trump saying in another post that the outlets’ reporting was “a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” The judge was unmoved by that argument. Kelly said it was clear from Trump’s announcement of the ban and from subsequent remarks that his motivation was content. “President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him,” Kelly wrote, finding this decision violated the journalists’ First and Fifth amendment rights. He noted, however, that his decision doesn’t concede that Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness are unfounded or that the government is “powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.” Kelly cited Trump’s recent remarks to Time magazine that he didn’t like “bad story after bad story” coming from CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists. It was, Ted Boutrous, the news outlets’ attorney, had argued ahead of the decision, “a confession of what amounts to viewpoint discrimination.” “President Trump, I’ll give him credit,” Boutrous said. “He’s not hiding it.” In his previous decision, Kelly also found that the administration had denied the outlets due process under settled law from several cases that have made their way to the D.C. federal appeals court. The White House argued that the appeals court decisions were wrong. “Maybe—but this Court is bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop,” Kelly wrote. At a hearing on the injunction Thursday, the Justice Department lawyer representing the White House, Michael Velchik, asked Kelly to lift his restraining order, calling the White House a “sacred place” that shouldn’t have to give people access just because they “identify as a reporter.” “Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” Velchik said. Boutrous argued that the administration was engaging in impermissible and unconstitutional “viewpoint discrimination” because the ban was based on Trump’s dislike of the outlets’ reporting and because he has said he hoped the ban would force journalists to “straighten themselves out.” In court filings, Boutrous urged Kelly to ignore the national security arguments, saying they were manufactured and not what the case is really about. Boutrous argued that “the President himself has continued telling anyone who will listen precisely what this ban is really about, most recently complaining at length in an interview with Time magazine that he banned Plaintiffs because he feels that he should not ‘be forced to bear’ what he considers ‘constantly bad stories,’ as he ‘won the election’ and has ‘done great things.’” After Tuesday night’s ruling, Boutrous said he and his clients were grateful to the court for securing their access anew. “The President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like,” he said in a statement. “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban.’” Separately, the Justice Department said last week that it was investigating five major TV networks, including CNN and NBC, for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of Trump as a result of the ban against the three news outlets. The pool is a rotating group of networks that share the duties of recording a president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The on-duty network then distributes information and media, such as video and audio, to other outlets for their use.

articles.title: Hinson, Turek tangle in fierce final Iowa Senate debate
articles.summary: Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D) squared off in a heated second and final debate for the open Iowa Senate seat on Tuesday. The pair, who clashed in their first debate last week, are locked in a toss-up race for outgoing Sen. Joni Ernst’s (R) seat in the upper chamber. Election forecasters have moved the race in…
articles.body:
Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D) squared off in a heated second and final debate for the open Iowa Senate seat on Tuesday.

The pair, who clashed in their first debate last week, are locked in a toss-up race for outgoing Sen. Joni Ernst’s (R) seat in the upper chamber. Election forecasters have moved the race in the ruby red state in Democrats’ favor, as Republicans face tough political headwind this cycle.

A Democrat has not been elected to the upper chamber since 2008, and the pair are neck-and-neck in the latest polls . Hinson is narrowly seen as the favorite to win in November, according to Decision Desk HQ .

The debate, hosted by Nexstar affiliate WHO 13 in Des Moines, largely focused on hot-button issues such as affordability and the war in Iran while the pair leaned on their usual attack points from the campaign trail. Nexstar also owns The Hill.

Notably, Hinson criticized President Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, joining a growing chorus of GOP lawmakers condemning the move. Farm states, like Iowa, have been hit hard as diesel prices have soared amid the war in Iran.

“We need to lower gas prices in this country. We need to lower diesel prices, but I don’t think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it,” Hinson said Tuesday, arguing the U.S. should instead lower the federal gas tax and consider a rebate program.

Hinson, who is endorsed by the president , has broken with Trump on some policy priorities on the campaign trail. Last month, she spoke out against the war in Iran, calling for an end to the months-long conflict.

Turek agreed with Hinson and expressed opposition to the president’s deal with Moscow but quickly hammered the House Republican’s votes against a war powers resolution to rein in the war in Iran.

“We are in this situation because of this unnecessary war in Iran that Ashley Hinson voted in favor of continuing seven times,” he said. “This has led to gas prices going up in Iowa more than almost any other state.”

Tuesday’s debate took a testy turn as attention shifted to the candidates’ personal finances and voting records.

“We have a corruption crisis that’s leading to an affordability crisis because we’re sending people like Ashley Hinson up to D.C. not to fight for the people of Iowa but to go up there and to make themselves more wealthy and to look out for the billionaires,” Turek said Tuesday.

Attack ads opposing Hinson have focused on her personal wealth, while the House Republican has sought to underscore her support for a congressional stock trading ban.

Turek has zeroed in on her growing wealth in Congress, particularly her husband’s 2021 sale of his insurance agency to a private equity company.

Hinson said Tuesday that she doesn’t own any publicly traded stocks, which is reflected in her personal financial disclosure filed in August, though she and her husband do report a list of mutual funds and ETFs.

“His lies are beneath him on this race, and he’s muddying the water because he does not want to talk about his own liberal record here,” Hinson responded, adding that the Democrat is “too liberal for Iowa.”

Hinson’s personal financial disclosure report shows that her spouse, Matt Arenholz, owns privately held stock from High Street Insurance Partners valued between $1 million and $5 million. The firm bought out the insurance company that Arenholz co-owned, according to PolitiFact. He received part of the sale.

“My husband sold his business, and private stock is not trading stock,” Hinson said after she was pressed again on the issue.

Hinson, meanwhile, took aim at Turek’s attendance record in the state legislature this session, saying “I’ve done more town halls than the percentage of time he showed up to work this year.”

“Forty-two percent of the time is all Rep. Turek showed up to work this year, and that’s two out of every five days of work,” Hinson said. “And I think Iowans, if you’re watching tonight, you should know if you don’t show up to work two out of five days, you’re not getting a promotion, you’re getting fired.”

PolitiFact found that the state lawmaker had missed 261 House floor votes out of 445 votes between Jan. 12 and April 2. PolitiFact noted that the number only includes votes before the full House and not committee or subcommittee votes.

An analysis of Turek’s attendance record by KTIV in August showed that the state lawmaker had missed 58 percent of votes on the House floor.

Turek acknowledged missing the votes when pressed, chalking it up to a busy campaign schedule.

“I’m out campaigning. I’m out meeting Iowans all over all 99 counties,” Turek said. “I’ve done hundreds of in-person town halls.”

articles.title: Trump administration slashes time refugees have to challenge loss of legal status
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland Security reduced the number of days refugees have to challenge their legal status revocation from 30 days to just 10.
articles.body: The Trump administration is adopting a new rule that would shorten the time refugees have to challenge the termination of their legal status, marking another restriction on legal immigration pathways as the White House continues its immigration enforcement crackdown. The new policy, which takes effect Wednesday without undergoing the usual advance public notice-and-comment process, reduces the time refugees have to respond to a notice of intent to terminate their status from 30 days to 10. According to the new rule, the administration is aiming to "mitigate potential risks" linked to people who were admitted as refugees but were not eligible for refugee status. The documents pointed to refugees admitted during the Biden administration, claiming there was an "alarming erosion of the integrity" of the refugee program during those years, although refugee advocates dispute that allegation. TRUMP ADMIN PAUSES VISA APPOINTMENTS WORLDWIDE AMID HEIGHTENED SCREENING FOR APPLICANTS "A review of refugee processing policies and procedures implemented under the Biden administration indicates an alarming erosion of integrity leading to aliens being admitted to the United States as refugees when their identities, eligibility for refugee classification, and admissibility were determined based on incomplete records," DHS' document reads. "The priority of expediency over quality encouraged a lack of robust interviews," it added. "Certain questions to ensure that aliens were eligible for refugee status prior to admission to the United States were omitted and this increased the risk of ineligible aliens being approved for refugee classification and subsequently admitted to the United States." A spokesman for Citizenship and Immigration Services, Zach Kahler, similarly said the agency has found "an alarming erosion of screening and vetting measures" during the Biden administration to "rush processing and maximize the number of refugees admitted." The Trump administration is "ensuring that refugee status is reserved only for those who were eligible under the law," he said in a statement to The Associated Press. This comes after the Trump administration ordered the review of at least 185,000 refugees admitted during the Biden administration who still have pending green card applications. The U.S. refugee admissions program has historically enjoyed bipartisan support since Congress passed the Refugee Act of 1980. Refugees undergo extensive security screenings and background checks before being approved for resettlement. Many spend years waiting in refugee camps before they can be admitted after undergoing multiple rounds of interviews and screenings. With the Trump administration's new rule, critics argue tens of thousands of people who fled persecution and wars in their home countries could be forced into deportation. "These families did everything asked of them," Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president of Global Refuge, said in a statement. "They submitted to interviews, background checks and years of waiting abroad, only setting foot on U.S. soil once government officials approved their applications." She said the Department of Homeland Security now wants to "revisit those decisions on a 10-day clock, a notice period wholly insufficient to find a lawyer, translate documents or get records out of a country they were forced to flee due to conflict or persecution." "In some cases, refugees may not even receive the notice before their ten days are up, effectively eliminating their only chance to respond," she added. "If the government’s case for termination is truly strong, it can afford to give people a meaningful chance to challenge it." HIAS, a major refugee aid group, also warned that refugees who have fled violence, persecution and displacement will be at risk of being deported to countries where they could be subject to persecution and torture. "They are trying to upend the core principle that refugee resettlement represents permanent protection," HIAS Vice President Naomi Steinberg said in a statement. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FINES OF UP TO $1.8M FOR MIGRANTS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Trump administration has significantly overhauled the U.S. refugee admissions program, sharply restricting overall admissions while prioritizing the resettlement of white South Africans. Last month, the Trump administration established a ceiling of 17,500 refugee admissions for fiscal year 2027, with most slots allocated to Afrikaners, a predominantly white ethnic group in South Africa. During his first term, President Donald Trump reduced the number of refugees approved every year. The Biden administration reversed that trend, setting a refugee admissions ceiling of 125,000 for fiscal year 2025. When Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, he immediately suspended the refugee program, stranding people around the world who had been set to come to the U.S. The administration later reopened the program but limited it mostly to white South Africans. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump announces massive oil, gas and mineral exploration plans in Greenland, touts national security benefits
articles.summary: President Donald Trump announced on Truth Social that experts say Greenland's oil reserves rival almost any land, but details remain unclear.
articles.body: President Donald Trump announced Wednesday that "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration was expected to begin in Greenland. "Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!" Trump posted on Truth Social. "There are Experts that are saying that the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the World and, even more importantly, from a Security Purpose in the Defense and Offense of both the United States of America, and Europe, is second to none," he continued. "Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived," Trump added. TRUMP'S GREENLAND FIXATION REVEALED AS WARS EXPOSE WHY THE ARCTIC ISLAND MATTERS NOW MORE THAN EVER Trump said Greenland "gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!" Trump did not immediately provide additional details about when or how the exploration would begin. Greenland's government stopped issuing new oil and gas exploration licenses in 2021, citing environmental and climate concerns. Some previously issued licenses remain valid, although drilling requires additional government approvals. Greenland is believed to hold significant untapped oil and gas resources, but commercially recoverable reserves have not been established. Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for comment. Trump's comments come after the U.S., Denmark and Greenland signed a new security agreement last month expanding U.S. military access to the strategically important Arctic island. While the U.S. already had extensive military rights in Greenland under a 1951 defense agreement, the new arrangement expands Washington's ability to establish additional military facilities, subject to consultation and procedures outlined in the agreement. SECURITY EXPERT HAILS TRUMP'S GREENLAND PACT AS A 'BIG DEAL' ON PAR WITH ALASKA PURCHASE The agreement also restricts military installations by non-NATO countries and establishes safeguards against potentially threatening foreign investments in sensitive sectors, including natural resources and critical infrastructure. Although Trump had sought to acquire Greenland, repeatedly arguing that U.S. ownership was necessary for national security, the new agreement did not grant U.S. sovereignty over the island. Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, with Copenhagen retaining authority over foreign, defense and security policy while Greenland controls many of its domestic affairs, including mineral resources.
