articles.title: María Prieto Vicente, CMO de Heymondo: "Un viaje contratado no te exime de formar parte de una mesa electoral"
articles.standfirst: La citación para formar parte de una mesa electoral puede obligar a cancelar un viaje
articles.summary: La citación para formar parte de una mesa electoral puede obligar a cancelar un viaje
articles.body: Tener un viaje contratado para la fecha de unas elecciones no exime automáticamente de formar parte de una mesa electoral. Esta es una de las cuestiones que deben tener en cuenta los viajeros ante una convocatoria electoral, especialmente si ya han reservado vuelos, hoteles u otros servicios que podrían suponer un perjuicio económico en caso de cancelación. María Prieto Vicente, Chief Marketing Officer (CMO) de la compañía de seguros de viaje Heymondo, explica qué ocurre en estos supuestos y en qué circunstancias una póliza puede cubrir los gastos derivados de la anulación de una reserva. La clave está en distinguir entre la decisión voluntaria de cancelar un viaje para votar presencialmente y la obligación de acudir a una mesa electoral. No son situaciones equivalentes y tampoco reciben el mismo tratamiento por parte de las aseguradoras. Quienes tengan un viaje reservado para el 29 de noviembre, día de las elecciones generales, y decidan cancelarlo para acudir presencialmente a las urnas no podrán acogerse, por norma general, a la cobertura de anulación por este motivo. "La decisión de acudir a votar de forma presencial no se contempla como una causa justificada en los seguros de viaje", explica María Prieto Vicente. La representante de Heymondo recuerda que el ordenamiento jurídico contempla el voto por correo para los ciudadanos que se encuentran fuera de su localidad o de viaje. En consecuencia, la cancelación voluntaria de una reserva para votar presencialmente responde a una elección individual, no a una obligación legal ineludible. Por eso, según detalla la responsable de marketing, "los seguros de cancelación no asumen los costes derivados de esta decisión". La situación es distinta cuando el viajero recibe una notificación oficial para formar parte de una mesa electoral y ya había contratado sus vacaciones o desplazamientos. En este caso, tener una reserva previa no supone quedar exento automáticamente de la obligación. "El viajero debe tramitar una alegación formal ante la Junta Electoral de Zona en el plazo de siete días desde la recepción de la citación", señala Prieto Vicente. La existencia de un viaje contratado con anterioridad a la convocatoria puede servir para solicitar la dispensa, especialmente si la cancelación supone un perjuicio económico importante. No obstante, presentar la alegación no garantiza que vaya a ser aceptada: corresponde a la Junta Electoral valorar las circunstancias y resolver la petición. La responsable de Heymondo cita entre los supuestos contemplados por la normativa la concurrencia de determinados eventos familiares de especial relevancia durante la jornada electoral, siempre que sean inaplazables o que su aplazamiento provoque perjuicios económicos importantes. En estos casos, la persona interesada debe acreditar documentalmente tanto la celebración prevista del evento como su carácter inaplazable o las consecuencias económicas de suspenderlo. ¿Cuándo entra en juego el seguro? Según explica Prieto Vicente, "es en caso de que la Junta Electoral desestime la alegación y mantenga la citación obligatoria cuando la cobertura de cancelación del seguro de viaje se activa", siempre que el viajero tenga contratada esa garantía y la póliza contemple el supuesto. Sí. Los suplentes también están obligados a comparecer en el colegio electoral, por lo que tener un viaje contratado no les permite ausentarse sin más. "El suplente está igualmente obligado a presentar la correspondiente solicitud de excusa ante la Junta Electoral de Zona", explica Prieto Vicente. Si la petición es rechazada, deberá acudir al colegio electoral y no podrá iniciar el viaje en las condiciones previstas. En ese caso, también podría recurrir a la cobertura de anulación, si la tiene contratada y se cumplen los requisitos establecidos en el seguro. La condición de suplente, por tanto, no elimina la obligación de comparecer ni impide solicitar la dispensa. Si la Junta Electoral rechaza la alegación y el viajero necesita cancelar su reserva, deberá acreditar tanto la citación como los gastos que no puede recuperar por otras vías. "Para gestionar la indemnización de los gastos de anulación de un viaje por esta causa, el asegurado debe remitir la citación oficial y la copia de la alegación presentada junto con la resolución de rechazo emitida por la Junta Electoral de Zona", detalla la representante de Heymondo. A esa documentación deberá añadir los justificantes de pago del viaje y los documentos que acrediten los importes no reembolsables o las penalizaciones aplicadas por la cancelación. Quienes ya tengan un viaje contratado, pero no hayan adquirido un seguro de cancelación, pueden tener la opción de contratar una póliza antes de recibir una eventual citación electoral. Sin embargo, el momento de la contratación es determinante. "Es posible contratar un seguro con cobertura de anulación siempre que la persona no haya recibido la notificación oficial de la citación para la mesa electoral", afirma Prieto Vicente. La responsable de marketing de Heymondo precisa que el hecho que origina el posible siniestro es la notificación personal al ciudadano, no el anuncio general de la convocatoria de elecciones. Por ello, si el seguro se contrata antes de recibir esa comunicación y se respetan los plazos y condiciones de la modalidad elegida, la citación posterior podría quedar cubierta.

articles.title: Sanctuary city whack-a-mole: Same policy, different ZIP code
articles.summary: Equal justice under law is supposed to mean something, and it isn’t that government discriminates against citizens in favor of illegal immigrants.
articles.body:
On Oct. 9, House Judiciary Republicans released a staff report on Colorado alleging that Denver’s sheriff ignored detainers from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement this year for people charged with crimes ranging from felony assault with a deadly weapon to sexual assault on a child .

The report names Fernando Barrios-Ramirez, a Venezuelan national accused of sexual assault on a child and kidnapping . He is presumed innocent. The report comes from the majority party, offering allegations and no victim count. No court has weighed in.

The question still stands: Why would any jail release a foreign national with an immigration detainer facing charges like these without a clean handoff to federal agents?

Congress has examined Fairfax County and Arlington County in Virginia and has now turned to Denver and Boulder. Whack one mole, and another pops up in the next blue county with the same policy and the same defense.

My thesis is that elected sheriffs and prosecutors owe their first duty to the residents who put them in office. When a policy protects accused violent offenders from a federal handoff, those officials should either defend that policy in public with data or else change it.

A sheriff isn’t a trustee in the legal sense, but the principle still applies. Marcus Aurelius wrote it in one line: “That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee.” Sanctuary politics protect one bee at the swarm’s expense.

A detainer is a request from ICE that no judge has signed. Colorado law bars local officers from holding someone solely on an ICE detainer , so the sheriffs who cite the law have a point. The real fight, therefore, is over the handoff.

On Feb. 28, 2025, Denver told ICE , with about 60 minutes’ notice, that it was releasing Abraham Gonzalez Romero, an alleged member of the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua prison gang. Mayor Mike Johnston later testified that six ICE agents showed up on the scene to pick him up. Federal prosecutors say that, as the Venezuelan national left the jail, he jumped a handrail and ran into an officer. Both fell . Gonzalez was charged with assaulting a federal officer. He is presumed innocent.

Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) asked why Denver had not released Gonzalez directly to ICE . He argued for a mandatory 48 hours’ notice when defendants with ICE detainers are released. That is a fair request, as an arrest made inside a secure jail is a lot safer to the public than a foot chase on a public sidewalk.

The prosecutor’s office is the second mole. The report says that a 2019 Denver policy directs prosecutors to mitigate immigration consequences, even in violent felony cases, and that District Attorney John Walsh has kept weighing those consequences. The committee’s complaint is that citizens charged with the same crime do not get softball plea-deals shaped by their risk of deportation.

Equal justice under law is supposed to mean something, and it isn’t that government discriminates against citizens in favor of illegal aliens.

Boulder District Attorney Michael Dougherty, who is running for attorney general , calls the report “a political stunt.” Jordan retorts that Dougherty has produced no documentation to back up his side of the story. Louis Brandeis wrote that sunlight is the best disinfectant . If these policies protect public safety, then let’s have Dougherty post the charging guidelines, the detainer log, the release times, and then an account of what happened to each person after release.

Walsh warns that mandatory reporting would erode trust between immigrant communities and police, which matters when victims and witnesses decide whether to call. The trust concern is real for a domestic violence victim dialing 911. But it doesn’t reach a jail cell, because a suspect charged with a violent felony is not a witness.

A March 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 97 percent of Democrats who favor some but not all deportations support removing illegal aliens who have committed violent crimes .

Courts won’t settle this. DeShaney v. Winnebago County held in 1989 that a state’s failure to protect someone from private violence does not violate the Due Process Clause. Imbler v. Pachtman gave prosecutors absolute immunity from federal civil-rights damages suits in 1976.

That leaves the ballot box and Congress.

Colorado voters get the first swing on Nov. 3. Amendment 81 would require law enforcement to notify the Department of Homeland Security within 72 hours of charging someone with a violent crime, or someone with a prior felony conviction, if the person is in the country illegally or his or her status cannot be determined. It requires 55 percent to pass .

The League of Women Voters opposes it over the presumption of innocence and the risk of error.

Congress can also do something. It can move on the Shut Down Sanctuary Policies Act , which the Judiciary Committee passed on March 5 . It would allow the victims of those released by sanctuary jurisdictions to sue for damages. Federal officials can meet Colorado’s law halfway, because the state limits honoring detainers unless federal officials present a judge-signed warrant or order . Seek a judge’s signature in every violent case and press for 48 hours notice instead of 60 minutes.

Sanctuary officials have spent years explaining whom their policies protect. The accused, they say, are safe and welcome. Fine, but residents would like to hear who is looking after them.

Congress will keep swinging at moles, because the holes are endless. The lasting fix belongs to the voters who hire these officials, and Colorado’s turn comes Nov. 3.

Jay Rogers is a financial professional with more than 30 years of experience in private equity, private credit, hedge funds, and wealth management.

articles.title: A warning from Pew: The 2026 midterms will be uniquely difficult for polls
articles.summary: A mix of factors is creating unprecedented challenges for polling and for the public trying to understand it.
articles.body:
Polls are again under scrutiny, with some rushing in to proclaim their demise. But it isn’t that polls have gotten worse. Rather, a mix of factors is creating unprecedented challenges for polling and for the public trying to understand it.

Why? First, there are the perennial challenges that are consistently misunderstood. Surveys are well suited to measure beliefs and attitudes about issues, and they can capture respondents’ candidate preferences pretty accurately. But predicting who will actually turn out to vote will always be an imperfect effort, largely because people are bad at predicting their own behavior and tend to report aspirations rather than realities.

This challenge is magnified in midterms and primaries, contests that often have lower turnout , localized dynamics and low information. And yet, many consumers expect a level of precision that polls can’t deliver. And the cycle of disappointment repeats.

Second, there are slow-growing issues that have compounded the problem over the past decade. The polling field has exploded with new entrants as low-cost opt-in polling has developed. At the same time, the rapid increase in the cost of high-quality polling has led to fewer of these polls, relative to cheaper opt-in polls. It’s harder to know which pollsters to trust, and some states and localities are left without reliable data for consumers.

Some opt-in pollsters have decent track records — their modeling techniques may have improved, or they make educated guesses. We don’t know because their methodology is often opaque.

But trust in opt-in polling is increasingly in question. Numerous recent studies have documented “ bogus respondents ” slipping into these surveys. Fake respondents — whether artificial intelligence-enabled bot farms or people trying to make money — are more sophisticated and harder to eliminate. It particularly affects estimates of Hispanic adults and young people — groups whose preferences and turnout may be decisive in November.

Meanwhile, predicting who will show up to vote keeps getting harder as voting rules (when, where and how to vote) change over time and across jurisdictions, and as microtargeting by campaigns can move segments of the electorate in ways broad polls often can’t register.

If any of this gives you pause, we still haven’t touched on three new wildcards this year.

First, we’re seeing more completely “ synthetic surveys ,” — polls that purport to measure public opinion but don’t actually survey humans. Instead, they use AI to model what people would say. Our research on synthetic surveys finds they are not reliable substitutes for public opinion. Separately, we have also seen polls being shared that are entirely fabricated without disclosure.

Second, uncertainty about voting mechanics, such as mail-in ballots, changing election laws in some states and even concerns about voter intimidation could influence turnout in hard-to-model ways. Widespread mid-cycle redistricting has scrambled voters’ awareness of who’s on their ballots. And the 2026 race has fewer incumbents on the ballot than any general election since 1992 .

Third, the issues of AI and data centers have swelled into the public dialogue but haven’t yet become completely polarized by party. This makes the impact of AI on elections more dependent on local conditions, such as planned or existing data centers nearby, and what candidates are saying about the issue.

In short, predicting who will vote has always been hard in lower turnout elections. It’s become more challenging over time, and 2026 has a swirl of unknowns compounding the challenge — a perfect storm ripe for confusion. Any one of these factors could yield surprises that are impossible to predict, even for the highest quality polls.

So, what can you do to make sense of the deluge of polls in this cycle? To start, don’t put too much stock in a single poll when thinking about election outcomes, and be wary of outliers.

Ask smart questions of the polls you do consider: Who conducted the poll? Does the organization have a good track record and reputation? Do they have a dog in the fight? Can you be sure the poll is surveying real humans? If so, which ones? Does the organization readily share information about its questions and methodology? Transparency is not the same as quality, but a lack of transparency is certainly a red flag.

Use polls for what they are best at: helping us understand the mood of the country, the issues on the public’s mind and what’s dividing and uniting people — in short, what the election is likely going to mean. Don’t expect polls to do what they cannot, especially this year.

Lastly, don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater: Don’t let a bad poll destroy your trust in polling altogether. Rigorous polls are still the best way to understand what the public thinks and believes even if they don’t always accurately predict primaries and midterms.

Without the public voice in polls, we’re left only with politicians claiming to speak for us.

Michael Dimock is president of Pew Research Center.

articles.title: Trump’s Supreme Court emergency docket scorecard, by the numbers
articles.summary: President Trump’s administration has filed 42 emergency pleas to the Supreme Court since retaking the White House — surpassing the count from his entire first term. And it doesn’t look like he’s hitting the brakes any time soon. Just last week, the Justice Department asked the justices to stop a ruling favoring Democrats in a fight…
articles.body:
President Trump ’s administration has filed 42 emergency pleas to the Supreme Court since retaking the White House — surpassing the count from his entire first term.

And it doesn’t look like he’s hitting the brakes any time soon. Just last week, the Justice Department asked the justices to stop a ruling favoring Democrats in a fight over TV advertising rates ahead of the midterms.

As the count ticks higher, we’re taking a look at Trump’s scorecard.

The TV ad rate case and another one concerning transgender inmates remain pending. Four others were withdrawn, leaving 36 emergency cases with an actual decision on the books.

Trump has effectively won 28 and lost eight, according to The Gavel’s analysis. That’s a nearly 80 percent success rate.

None of those wins was unanimous, however.

The Supreme Court justices often publicly highlight that the majority of decisions on their regular docket, called the “merits docket,” are unanimous. The court frequently acts unanimously in low-profile emergency disputes, too.

But when it comes to the president’s emergency requests, the justices’ ideological lines are clear.

Here’s a look at the 36 decided cases by apparent vote count:

Disclaimer: A justice can dissent in an emergency case without disclosing it (sometimes called a “stealth dissent”). This is based on dissents revealed publicly.

The four unanimous decisions? One was moot, another was cleared out after the justices decided an overlapping case, and the other two were unanimous losses for the administration.

He can blame Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson for that. She’s the only one of the court’s liberals to have publicly dissented against him every time he’s won.

Jackson has made no secret of her detestation for the Trump administration’s emergency docket tactics. It’s the subject of a lecture she regularly gives while traveling the country, and in opinions, she has called her colleagues’ decisions “ Calvinball jurisprudence ,” “ hubristic and senseless ” and a “ Kafkaesque nightmare .”

The two other liberal justices, Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan, are sometimes aligned with Jackson, but the duo didn’t sign onto that searing prose.

In a few cases, they haven’t noted a dissent at all.

Sotomayor didn’t in two of Trump’s wins: at early stages of lawsuits over cutbacks to temporary protected status and large-scale government layoffs.

Kagan didn’t in four: those two Sotomayor cases, plus a battle over probationary employee firings and a challenge to Trump ending a Biden-era parole program .

To be clear, Trump hasn’t always won. And some of his eight losses were sizable:

The justices declined the administration’s pleas to freeze nearly $2 billion in foreign aid payments; reverse a whistleblower office head’s reinstatement; block the return of Kilmar Ábrego Garcia after his mistaken deportation to El Salvador; greenlight the firing of the Federal Reserve’s Lisa Cook; block a lawsuit over immigration judges’ public speech restrictions; deploy the National Guard in Chicago; re-fire the nation’s top copyright official ; and, most recently, OK his mail-in voting plan for the midterms.

The Supreme Court’s emergency docket is not new — for example, the court has long considered last-ditch efforts to stave off executions — but it has surged in activity during Trump’s presidencies.

The president’s critics say his flood of appeals reflects that he is acting lawlessly. Trump and his supporters say lower judges stymying the president’s agenda are the ones at fault and are forcing the administration’s hand.

Regardless of who is right, emergency cases now dominate the court’s work.

So, let’s look at the scorecard for those lower judges. Trump’s emergency docket wins have stopped more than a dozen.

Four judges have seen it happen more than once. Most of them serve on the bench in Boston: Brian Murphy and Myong Joun , both appointees of former President Biden , and Indira Talwani , an appointee of former President Obama . Edward Chen , an Obama appointee who serves in San Francisco, rounds out the leaderboard.

Just four of Trump’s 28 wins pushed back on a district judge appointed by a Republican president.

That’s no surprise. After all, litigants are concentrating their lawsuits in favorable districts, which are frequently assigned to judges appointed by Democratic presidents, who have repeatedly ruled against the president.

Welcome to The Gavel, The Hill’s weekly newsletter unpacking the intersection of courts & politics from Zach Schonfeld and S ophie Brams . Email us tips at zschonfeld@thehill.com and sbrams@thehill.com . You can also reach out to us on X (@ZachASchonfeld and @sophiebrams) or Signal (zachschonfeld.48 and sbrams.32).

Trump ads blocked: The Trump administration was ordered by a federal judge in New York to immediately stop airing political ads featuring the president. A watchdog group, union and others have challenged the campaign as an unlawful use of government funds.

White House media ban : The Trump administration cannot bar CNN, Politico and MS NOW from accessing the White House while their lawsuit challenging the media ban continues, a federal judge has ruled

DOJ in hot seat: A federal judge in Washington, D.C., told Justice Department lawyers Monday that she was “furious” and “beyond disappointed” after hundreds of trees were abruptly cut down at East Potomac Park with less than a day’s notice. The judge has ordered a pause in tree removal through at least Oct. 26 while she weighs a longer injunction.

Trump’s triumphal arch challenged: The county of Arlington, Va., is suing the Trump administration to block construction of a proposed 250-foot arch in the nation’s capital.

Tupac murder mastermind sentenced: Duane “Keffe D” Davis has been sentenced to 40 years in prison after he was found guilty of orchestrating the drive-by shooting that killed rapper Tupac Shakur in 1996

The Justice Department’s Office of Immigration Litigation, which handles all civil immigration cases, has seen its caseload jump to record highs under the second Trump administration despite a dwindling number of attorneys. Our colleague Rebecca Beitsch took a look at the data.

Scrutiny surrounding the high-profile sexual assault investigation at Cornell University has intensified with the appointment of New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) as a special prosecutor. Our colleague Lexi Lonas Cochran has more .

White House press pool fight turns to antitrust

President Trump ’s longstanding feud with the media is escalating again.

The Justice Department announced over the weekend that it is opening an antitrust investigation into the country’s five major television networks after they briefly suspended pool coverage in solidarity with outlets that were barred from the White House.

The networks — NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — stopped providing shared video coverage of the president’s daily activities for several days last month in response to Trump’s decision to revoke the badges of CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists.

Pool coverage resumed after a federal judge ordered access be immediately restored, but the White House has since barred CNN and Politico from fulfilling their duties, including aboard Air Force One.

A spokesperson for the Justice Department said it is examining whether the pause violated federal antitrust law, calling it a “group boycott among commercial competitors.”

The underlying legal principle is found in Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, a law passed during the peak of the industrial revolution that was intended to curb anti-competitive practices and rein in monopolies.

It reads, in part: “Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is declared to be illegal.”

Federal agencies like the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) assert that group boycotts can become illegal when they are used to fix prices, restrict or disadvantage competition or jointly target a certain entity.

“Any company may, on its own, refuse to do business with another firm, but an agreement among competitors not to do business with targeted individuals or businesses may be an illegal boycott, especially if the group of competitors working together has market power,” FTC guidance states.

The distinction has been heavily parsed in the courts.

In a landmark 1911 Supreme Court case called Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, the court interpreted the Sherman Act to prohibit only unreasonable or undue restraints of trade rather than all restraints.

To determine whether the agreement crosses that threshold, the justices adopted a standard known as the “rule of reason.” It weighs the anticompetitive harms of a practice against its commercial benefits by analyzing factors like purpose and market power.

But courts have also treated some agreements as “per se” violations, which are so blatantly anti-competitive that they can be found automatically illegal without the balancing test.

It remains an open question how either approach could be applied to the pool coverage scenario, as courts have historically distinguished between economic boycotts and purely political ones.

The high court found in a 1990 case that a group of private lawyers in D.C. committed antitrust violations when they agreed to stop providing legal services to indigent defendants until the city raised their fees. Years earlier, the court concluded that a socio-politically-motivated, NAACP-led boycott of white-owned businesses in Mississippi was protected by the First Amendment.

The television networks have not publicly addressed the investigation but previously said in a joint statement that “no administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”

Cases the Supreme Court is taking up — or passing on — this term.

IN: DOGE, ‘material support’ for terrorists

The Supreme Court took up three new cases Tuesday. We previewed all of them in previous editions as ones to watch:

In U.S. Doge Service v. U.S. District Court for D.C. , the justices will consider the Trump administration’s efforts to stave off a judge’s demand that the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) turn over documents to shed light on whether it must respond to public records requests.

The high court on its emergency docket already sided with the administration at an earlier stage of the case. Now, they’re taking it up on their normal docket.

In Blanche v. Ozurumba, the court will review whether a Nigerian man’s cooking for a terrorist group while in captivity amounted to “material support” for the group, making him ineligible for asylum.

And in Berry v. United States, the court will wade into when criminal defendants bringing habeas petitions are entitled to appeal rejected arguments.

It’s a thorny issue, but it’s one that matters to Dave Clark , a former real estate executive commuted by Trump. He had a similar petition pending with the justices, which they’re holding onto.

OUT: Sotomayor, Gorsuch join forces on immigration

Last week, we told you to keep an eye on Herrera-Salazar v. United States .

A Mexican man was arguing it violated his double jeopardy rights to prosecute him a second time for illegally reentering the country while he was still on supervised release for the first conviction. That barred him from leaving U.S. soil.

The court turned away the man’s case, but it only came over a harsh rebuke of the government’s conduct from both a liberal and conservative justice.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor — an appointee of former President Obama — joined by Justice Neil Gorsuch — an appointee of President Trump — called it “ constitutional absurdity .”

“Because I hope the facts of this case are anomalous and because Herrera-Salazar has since been removed from the United States, I concur in the Court’s decision not to grant review in this case,” Sotomayor wrote.

Petitions for the Supreme Court to take up cases we are keeping a close eye on …

Roberto Clemente trademark: Puerto Rico made $15 million off license plates branded with imagery of baseball legend Roberto Clemente. His sons say it misappropriated his legacy and want the Supreme Court to reverse a partial loss dismissing some of their claims against Puerto Rico officials. The case is Clemente Properties, Inc v. Pierluisi-Urrutia .

Race-neutral admissions: The court has its latest opportunity to take up whether their decision invalidating affirmative action in college admissions also blocks schools from using race-neutral criteria to encourage diversity. The court previously turned away a similar case concerning a top-ranked high school in Virginia just outside the nation’s capital. Now, the issue has arisen on the other side of the city on the Maryland side of the border. The case is Association for Education Fairness, Petitioner v. Montgomery County Board of Education.

Sex offenders on Halloween: Missouri law requires convicted sex offenders to remain inside on Halloween, avoid contact with children, turn off outdoor lights and post a sign saying, “No candy or treats at this residence.” A man convicted of sodomizing a teenage girl — and later of violating the Halloween law — says it compels his speech in violation of the First Amendment. Missouri’s attorney general wants to revive the law.

Home distilling ban: Federal law makes it a felony to distill spirits in a home . The Trump administration appeals a ruling found it unconstitutional, rejecting the notion that the provision is necessary and proper for Congress to carry out its power to tax the beverages. A defendant charged in a different court, which ruled the other way, appeals in his case. The cases are Department of Justice v. McNutt and Ream v. Department of the Treasury.

The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in Salazar v. Paramount Global , a case concerning whether the Video Privacy Protection Act protects consumers who subscribe to any of a company’s products or only those who subscribe to its audiovisual ones.

A federal judge in D.C. will hold a hearing in a lawsuit brought by the National Democratic Committee which seeks to block the Trump administration from using taxpayer money to fund political ads.

An evidentiary hearing is scheduled in the murder retrial of Alex Murdaugh , who is accused in the 2021 killings of his wife and son in South Carolina.

The Supreme Court will release an orders list with actions in pending appeals.

A federal judge in D.C. will hear testimony from Trump administration officials in a dispute over the removal of hundreds of trees in East Potomac Park.

A federal judge in California will hear arguments in a lawsuit from two nurses unions seeking to block armed immigration officers from conducting enforcement at polling places during the midterms.

A federal judge in Massachusetts will hold a hearing to decide whether to resolve the state’s challenge to Medicaid work requirements provision passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act without a full trial.

A federal judge in Washington will hear arguments as the Trump administration seeks to dismiss a lawsuit from 15 Democratic-led states over a Day 1 executive order declaring a national energy emergency .

articles.body:
The Supreme Court will hear arguments Wednesday in a case testing whether a decades-old privacy law extends to consumers who subscribe to services unrelated to video content.

The case stems from a lawsuit against Paramount Global by a subscriber to a college sports newsletter who alleges the company improperly shared his video viewing history with Facebook for targeted advertising.

At issue is whether the 1988 Video Privacy Protection Act protects subscribers to any of a company’s products or only its audiovisual offerings.

The justices’ ruling could have broad implications for online privacy and future lawsuits involving digital tracking technology.

Oral arguments are scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. EDT.

articles.body:
Inflation rose in September, giving Republicans no relief as they campaign to retain both chambers of Congress. Consumer prices rose 3.7 percent , compared with a year earlier, up from 3.4 percent in August, according to Labor Department data released Wednesday morning.

President Trump is set to make back-to-back campaign stops in Arizona and Montana on Wednesday afternoon as he continues his multiday, multistate midterm blitz primarily targeting red states.

Trump is slated to speak in Bullhead City, Ariz., at 4 p.m. EDT before flying to Kalispell, Mont., for another speech at 8:15 p.m. The trip comes a day after the president made a rare campaign visit to Alaska. During the rally, he announced pardons for two men who were convicted of violating the Clean Air Act.

Meanwhile, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will give remarks alongside acting Army Secretary Adam Telle — who was tapped for the position in early September following the resignation of Dan Driscoll, who left his post after months of reported discord with the Pentagon chief.

Tille, who previously served as the assistant secretary of the Army for Civil Works, made his first public appearance as acting Army secretary on Monday. He will appear alongside Hegseth and acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao at 10 a.m. EDT.

Sprinkled throughout the evening will be several midterm election debates, including for the gubernatorial races in Maine and Iowa, both set for 8 p.m. Alaska’s candidates for Senate will then debate at 10 p.m.

But unlike these nominees, Democrat James Talarico will take the stage without his opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), in the Lone Star State’s Senate race. Talarico will appear in a televised town hall at 8 p.m., hosted by CNN and Jubilee Media, after repeatedly challenging Paxton to a debate.

The appearance comes after both the GOP candidate and Trump peddled theories surrounding Talarico’s two-week absence from the campaign trail — which the Democrat attributed to a flu diagnosis.

articles.title: Trump’s authoritarian raid on Ilhan Omar is an attack on the rule of law
articles.summary: The party that once so loudly complained about Democratic “lawfare” is now passively mute as Trump misuses Homeland Security resources in an attempt to unlawfully deport a sitting member of Congress who legally received asylum in this country.
articles.body:
When federal immigration agents raided Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minn.) home on Monday morning, right-wing media outlet Fox News broke the story almost as it happened. Despite most federal raids unfolding in tight secrecy, Fox’s reporting cited multiple sources at the Department of Homeland Security who seemed eager to spill sensitive details that cast Omar in a negative light.

It is no secret that the Somali-born Omar has been one of President Trump’s most consistent and vocal foes since the earliest days of his political career. Trump has returned her attacks with relish: last year he urged Omar to leave the country . And in February, he responded to Omar’s heckling at the State of the Union by demanding she be deported along with Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.).

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar posted on X in the hours following the raid. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”

Trump is no stranger to verbal warfare. Even so, it’s hard to see an ICE raid on Omar’s private residence as anything other than a stark escalation in Trump’s use of government power to retaliate against his countless Democratic enemies . The misuse of government resources on this scale should prompt bipartisan investigations and a wave of resignations. But in this morally rotten Republican Party, it will probably win some Trump toady the Medal of Freedom.

If Trump’s goal is to silence Omar, he fundamentally misunderstands both Omar and the limits of authoritarianism. In his race to silence any and all Democrats who dare to speak out about his abuses of power, Trump has succeeded only in weakening the rule of law and exposing Republicans as a party of small people willing to shred our liberties for their own short-term political gain.

The justification behind the raid is nonsensical, but as Trump’s failed prosecutions of New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) and former FBI director James Comey have shown, coherent legal arguments are only of secondary concern. Trump’s paper-thin reasoning seems to center on immigration paperwork filled out by Omar’s father when she was just a child — though even Trump’s allies can’t explain why Omar, who would have been 12 years old at the time, would bear legal liability for documents signed by her father.

Also at issue is the persistent rumor, popular on right-wing message boards, that Omar committed marriage and immigration fraud by marrying her brother. Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) even threatened to subpoena Omar earlier this year over the rumor, which has been a favorite of Trump’s since at least 2019 . Republican media influencers have ginned up plenty of controversy about Omar’s marital status, but they have repeatedly come up short on evidence.

But the scandals cooked up against Omar by Trump’s political network are beside the point. Trump doesn’t hate Omar because her father possibly misstated facts on a document from 1995. He hates her because she, like Comey and James, is a vocal critic of his policy failures and his brazen criminality. Ever the fanboy for dictators , Trump knows that the only way to silence some critics is by crushing them under the fist of weaponized government power.

Trump’s latest attempt to shut up a prominent critic would be easier to hide if he hadn’t made such a habit of it over the past year and a half. In fact, Trump’s inept misuse of power might be the defining characteristic of his second term.

He botched his effort to prosecute Federal Reserve chairman Jerome Powell and fell short in his attempt to censure Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), charge Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) with mortgage fraud , and prosecute Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) for urging soldiers to resist illegal orders. Before Omar, Trump busied himself with an almost certainly doomed federal investigation into California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D). And of course, add Comey and James to the list.

That Trump’s efforts almost inevitably fail doesn’t excuse Republicans from speaking up about his habitual abuse of government resources to harass his political rivals. The party that once so loudly complained about Democratic “ lawfare ” is now passively mute as Trump misuses Homeland Security resources in an attempt to unlawfully deport a sitting member of Congress who legally received asylum in this country.

That’s the stuff of Soviet nightmares, not American greatness.

Max Burns is a veteran Democratic strategist and founder of Third Degree Strategies.

articles.title: Trump takes a wrecking ball to legal representation for immigrant children
articles.summary: For decades, HHS has contracted with legal service providers to handle court representation and mandated for the kids. Now it has stopped paying many of them.
articles.body:
William Shakespeare’s famous line in Henry IV — “The first thing we do, let’s kill all the lawyers” — depicted a peasants’ rebellion against a tyrannical monarchy. The rebels realized that in order to achieve their objective, they first had to eliminate those who knew the rules and could stand in the way of a lawless mob.

Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., himself a lawyer, may know something about this strategy. He seems to be using it against immigrant children.

On September 29, in a nondescript notice published in the Federal Register, Kennedy announced the creation of a new department in the general counsel’s office named the “Unaccompanied Alien Children Representation Division,” which is supposed to “operate[] as a legal service provider for unaccompanied alien children.” Translated, the Trump administration will now use its own lawyers to go up against its own lawyers in deportation proceedings involving children before immigration judges employed by the Department of Justice. Trump sits atop of all of the actors in this play. The kids don’t stand a fighting chance.

Immigration proceedings are considered civil, not criminal, in nature, so the Sixth Amendment right to counsel does not apply. But Congress half-heartedly acknowledged that immigrant children need lawyers in the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, which directs that “[t]o the greatest extent practicable, the Secretary of Health and Human Services shall ensure that unaccompanied alien children . . . have access to counsel to represent them in legal proceedings or matters and protect them from mistreatment, exploitation, and trafficking.”

“To the greatest extent possible” is hardly a guarantee. But in a subsequent rule , HHS explicitly mandated that immigrant children get “[l]egal services information regarding the availability of free legal assistance, and that they may be represented by counsel at no expense to the government, the right to a removal hearing before an immigration judge; the ability to apply for asylum … in the first instance, and the ability to request voluntary departure in lieu of removal.”

Many of the 20,000 children who appear in immigration courts each year have no counsel. And so for decades, HHS has contracted with legal service providers such as the Acacia Center for Justice to handle court representation and mandated know-your-rights briefings for the kids.

Then, last November, the Trump administration stopped paying many legal nonprofits if they refused to turn over confidential information about their pediatric clients. These children will now be represented either by Trump HHS lawyers in the new division created by Kennedy or by OUR Rescue — a controversial organization originally founded by the former Trump advisor involved in the 2023 film “The Sound of Freedom,” which was promoted heavily by conservative media.

OUR Rescue is not a law office and has no competency to represent these children, yet Trump’s administration somehow gave it a $158 million sole-source, no-bid contract to do just that. Also receiving a no-bid contract to the Burke Law Group , whose principal worked for Trump in his first administration. The firm does energy law, not immigration.

The Acacia Center for Justice has filed a bid protest. But in the meantime, there is a legitimate concern that these children will not receive effective counsel. With either the Trump administration itself or a Trump-adjacent organization now on both sides of these children’s immigration proceedings, their Fifth Amendment right to due process becomes farcical.

When young kids show up in court alone, judges usually at least feel an obligation to ensure that they understand what is going on and are treated fairly. With a government “lawyer” now at the podium on their behalf, that incentive could dissipate. Moreover, Trump administration lawyers’ involvement likely means that the deportation process will move along more quickly and efficiently, in keeping with the Trump’s obsession over accelerated mass deportations .

For the lawyers involved, the dual representation violates numerous standards of professional conduct. This includes their obligation not to represent a client if it would involve a concurrent conflict of interest, not to reveal confidential information regarding a client (here, to the Trump administration) without the client’s consent (which young children cannot give), not to allow someone paying a lawyer (here, the Trump administration) to direct how their professional judgment is exercised (lest they lose their jobs), and to zealously represent minor children whose capacity to make decisions is by definition diminished.

Meanwhile, pre-verbal toddlers as young as two are routinely issued notices to appear for removal proceedings and are increasingly showing up without legal representation. They cannot read forms, comprehend charges of “removability,” or articulate viable legal claims like fear of persecution. Courtroom reporting has described kids playing with microphones, drawing on benches, and crying while judges attempt to conduct official proceedings.

Statistics show that children’s deportation rates go from over 80 percent to just 12 percent if they are represented by counsel. As Nelson Mandela rightly said, the true character of a society is revealed in how it treats its children. By that metric, America under Trump is an abject failure. We must do better.

Kimberly Wehle is currently a thematic group coordinator and fellow at the Netherlands Institute for Advanced Study in the Humanities and Social Sciences and author of “How to Read the Constitution — and Why,” as well as “What You Need to Know About Voting — and Why” and “How to Think Like a Lawyer — and Why. “

articles.title: ICE officer appeared to intentionally strike man with vehicle in Houston: Prosecutor
articles.summary: Texas prosecutors said they are weighing criminal charges after they alleged an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer appeared to intentionally hit a man with a vehicle in Houston over the weekend. Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old undocumented immigrant, was driving to work Saturday morning when federal authorities attempted to pull him over in unmarked…
articles.body:
Texas prosecutors said they are weighing criminal charges after they alleged an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer appeared to intentionally hit a man with a vehicle in Houston over the weekend.

Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old undocumented immigrant, was driving to work Saturday morning when federal authorities attempted to pull him over in unmarked vehicles, according to Cesar Espinosa, the executive director of immigrant rights group FIEL Houston.

Parra Hernandez stopped his car, and he and his passenger attempted to run away. ICE said in a statement to The Texas Tribune Saturday that Parra Hernandez was struck after he ran in front of one of the unmarked cars. However, surveillance footage from this incident shows the two men running away while an SUV veers and hits Parra Hernandez.

Espinosa said in a Monday statement that Parra Hernandez would need to undergo surgery, as his leg was broken in three places as a result of the collision.

“We demand answers and transparency from all agencies involved,” the FIEL executive director said. “The community needs to know the identities of the agents and if there are charges that are filed for the wrongdoing committed.”

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, announced Monday that his office had opened an investigation into the alleged use of force and requested assistance from the community.

“ICE tactics in our community are growing more brazen and more dangerous,” Teare said in a statement shared on social media. “High-speed pursuits and aggressive operations on busy streets put everyone at risk. No badge puts anyone above the law in Harris County and we will continue to follow evidence wherever it may lead.”

Teare told local outlet ABC13 on Tuesday he believed the ICE agent intentionally struck Parra Hernandez with his vehicle and that “a charging decision is going to come in a relatively short order in this case.”

This incident follows the July fatal ICE-involved shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston. Additionally, an ICE agent shot and injured Wilber Rafael Garces Perez last month in Austin while he was working as a food delivery driver in the city. Both of these incidents are currently under investigation.

The Hill has reached out to DHS and ICE for comment.
